questions.stem: A 79 year old man has had a productive cough for 3 days. Today his wife found him muddled and he has not passed urine since the morning. His temperature is 35.4°C, pulse rate 116 bpm, BP 94/58 mmHg, respiratory rate 26 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 92% breathing air.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Infection with organ dysfunction (confusion, oliguria, hypotension) is sepsis; hypothermia is as worrying as fever.

steps.x: Infection, low temperature, confusion and low urine output.

elim: Does not cause hypotension, confusion or oliguria.
No oedema or orthopnoea; fever source and low temperature suggest infection.
No exposure history; he has an infective source.
Does not explain productive cough with hypothermia and oliguria.

steps.x: E: Sepsis. Infection plus organ dysfunction = sepsis; hypothermia counts.

questions.stem: A 55 year old woman with an obstructed infected kidney has received 30 mL/kg of IV crystalloid. Her temperature is 39.2°C, pulse rate 128 bpm and BP 80/46 mmHg. Her urine output is 10 mL per hour and lactate 4.6 mmol/L.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Sepsis with persistent hypotension despite adequate fluid resuscitation is septic shock, needing vasopressors.

clues: urine output is 10 mL per hour
steps.x: Hypotension that persists after full fluid resuscitation.

elim: No cardiac cause; fever and infected kidney point to sepsis.
Fluid has been given without response.
There is organ dysfunction and shock.

steps.x: E: Septic shock. Persistent hypotension despite fluids = septic shock.

questions.stem: A 47 year old man has fever and dysuria for 2 days. He is alert. His temperature is 38.7°C, respiratory rate 20 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 97% breathing air. Another observation would immediately make him high risk for sepsis.
questions.q: Which finding would place him at high risk?
questions.e: High-risk criteria include systolic BP <90 mmHg, MAP <65, HR >131, RR >25 and responding only to voice or pain.

steps.x: An infection with no red flags yet.

elim: Raised but below the high-risk threshold of >131.
Fever alone is not a high-risk criterion.

steps.x: D: Systolic BP 86 mmHg. Systolic BP below 90 mmHg is a high-risk sepsis criterion.

questions.stem: A 68 year old woman with known hypertension has a 2 day history of cough and fever. Her usual BP is 168/90 mmHg. Today her BP is 122/70 mmHg, temperature 38.4°C, pulse rate 108 bpm and respiratory rate 22 breaths per minute. She is alert.
questions.q: Which feature places her at high risk of severe sepsis?
o: Fall in systolic BP of more than 40 mmHg
questions.e: A fall of more than 40 mmHg from baseline systolic is high risk even if the reading looks normal.

steps.x: Her BP looks normal but has fallen 46 mmHg.

elim: Below the high-risk heart rate threshold.
Fever alone is not a high-risk criterion.

steps.x: B: Fall in systolic BP of more than 40 mmHg. A >40 mmHg fall from baseline is a high-risk criterion.

questions.stem: A 39 year old woman receiving chemotherapy for breast cancer had her last cycle 9 days ago. She now has rigors and feels faint. Her temperature is 38.8°C, pulse rate 124 bpm, BP 88/52 mmHg and respiratory rate 24 breaths per minute.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Immunosuppression (here chemotherapy causing neutropenia) is a major risk factor for sepsis.

steps.x: Fever and shock at the nadir after chemotherapy.

elim: Does not cause fever and hypotension.
Does not explain neutropenia and rigors.
Occurs earlier and causes metabolic, not septic, features.

steps.x: C: Neutropenic sepsis. Immunosuppression is a key sepsis risk factor.

questions.stem: A 62 year old man is admitted with sepsis from a perforated appendix. He has no liver disease and was well a week ago. His CRP is 310 mg/L.
questions.q: Which is the most likely additional finding on his bloods?
questions.e: The liver diverts protein synthesis towards CRP and other acute-phase proteins, so albumin falls.

steps.x: High CRP in a man with a normal liver.
B: Low serum albumin. Low albumin is a further sign of sepsis.

questions.stem: An 86 year old woman from a care home has been off her food and newly confused for a day. Her temperature is 37.0°C, pulse rate 112 bpm, BP 96/60 mmHg and respiratory rate 24 breaths per minute. Urine dipstick shows leucocytes and nitrites.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Confusion, tachycardia, low BP and raised lactate with a urinary source is sepsis even without fever.

steps.x: Infection plus confusion and hypoperfusion, no fever needed.

elim: Gradual decline, not a 1 day illness with tachycardia.
She has organ dysfunction and a raised lactate.
Does not explain positive urine dipstick and raised lactate.
Glucose not low; dipstick shows infection.

steps.x: E: Sepsis from a urinary source. Elderly patients may present with confusion and no fever.

questions.stem: A 28 year old woman has a 2 day history of fever and loin pain. She is drowsy and opens her eyes only when spoken to. Her temperature is 39.4°C, pulse rate 118 bpm, BP 104/66 mmHg and respiratory rate 22 breaths per minute.
questions.q: Which feature most clearly places her in the high-risk sepsis group?
questions.e: Being responsive only to voice or pain (or unresponsive) is a high-risk sepsis criterion.

clues: opens her eyes only when spoken to
steps.x: Her conscious level is reduced.

elim: Points to the source, not severity.
Fever is not a high-risk criterion.

steps.x: D: Responding only to voice. Altered mental state is a red flag in sepsis.

questions.stem: A 71 year old man with type 2 diabetes and chronic kidney disease has a hot, swollen left foot ulcer. He is now confused. His temperature is 38.9°C, pulse rate 134 bpm, BP 92/56 mmHg and respiratory rate 26 breaths per minute. His lactate is 4.1 mmol/L.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: A dysregulated response to infection causing organ dysfunction is sepsis; chronic disease such as diabetes and CKD raises the risk.

clues: type 2 diabetes and chronic kidney disease
steps.x: An infected ulcer, risk factors, organ dysfunction.

elim: Not infective; does not cause shock.
Ketones and glucose are not described; foot infection explains it.
Does not cause confusion and raised lactate.
Would need very high glucose; infection and shock dominate.

steps.x: E: Sepsis. Infection plus organ dysfunction = sepsis.

questions.stem: A 64 year old woman with sepsis from cholangitis has received IV antibiotics and 2 L of IV fluid. She is warm to touch with a bounding pulse. Her temperature is 39.2°C, pulse rate 126 bpm, BP 78/40 mmHg and mean arterial pressure 53 mmHg. Her urine output is 5 mL per hour.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Warm vasodilated shock with low urine output persisting despite fluids is septic shock.

clues: warm to touch with a bounding pulse
steps.x: Vasodilated, hypotensive despite fluids.

elim: Warm peripheries and bounding pulse suggest vasodilation, not pump failure.
No bleeding; peripheries would be cold.

steps.x: E: Septic shock. Persistent hypotension after fluids = septic shock.

questions.stem: A 33 year old man is reviewed in clinic. He is a kidney transplant recipient on tacrolimus and prednisolone. The registrar explains which of his features most increases his risk of developing sepsis if he develops an infection.
questions.q: Which is his most important risk factor for sepsis?
questions.e: Infection is the most important risk factor, then immunosuppression and chronic disease.

steps.x: He is on immunosuppressants.

elim: Young age is not a risk factor.

steps.x: C: Immunosuppressive therapy. Immunosuppression increases sepsis risk.

questions.stem: A 58 year old man has fever, rigors and a productive cough. His temperature is 38.8°C, pulse rate 118 bpm, BP 98/60 mmHg and respiratory rate 24 breaths per minute. He is alert. The team wants a single test which, with the clinical picture, confirms sepsis with hypoperfusion.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation?
questions.e: The gold standard is a clinical diagnosis plus lactate; a raised lactate shows hypoperfusion.

clues: fever, rigors and a productive cough
steps.x: Hypoperfusion is the key question.

elim: Not the key test in UK practice.
Takes days and identifies the organism only.

steps.x: D: Serum lactate. Clinical diagnosis plus lactate.

questions.stem: A 74 year old woman has a 2 day history of fever and right upper quadrant pain and is jaundiced. Her temperature is 39.0°C, pulse rate 122 bpm and BP 90/56 mmHg. IV access has been obtained and IV antibiotics are prescribed.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation before the antibiotics are given?
questions.e: Blood cultures are taken before antibiotics where possible, as antibiotics may alter culture results, without delaying treatment beyond 1 hour.

clues: fever and right upper quadrant pain
steps.x: Antibiotics are about to be given.

elim: A treatment for source control, later.

steps.x: A: Blood cultures. Cultures before antibiotics, but do not delay antibiotics.

questions.stem: A 50 year old man with type 1 diabetes is drowsy with a fever and cough. His temperature is 38.6°C, pulse rate 120 bpm, BP 92/58 mmHg and respiratory rate 28 breaths per minute. The team wants rapid bedside information on acid-base balance, lactate, potassium and glucose.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate initial investigation?
questions.e: A blood gas gives acid-base balance, lactate, electrolytes and glucose within minutes.

clues: acid-base balance, lactate, potassium and glucose
steps.x: All four values come from one test.

elim: Identifies organism, not acid-base or electrolytes.
Does not give acid-base or lactate.
Does not give acid-base or lactate.

steps.x: B: Blood gas. Blood gas gives pH, lactate, electrolytes and sugar.

questions.stem: A 77 year old man is treated for sepsis with IV antibiotics after blood cultures. He has no localising symptoms. Examination shows coarse crackles at the right base. His temperature is 38.5°C, pulse rate 110 bpm and BP 100/62 mmHg. Chest X-ray (see item resources).

visual.title: Chest X-ray
visual.caption: Right lower zone consolidation: pneumonia as the source.

questions.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation to identify the source?
questions.e: A septic screen identifies the source; crackles point to pneumonia, so a chest X-ray is next.

clues: coarse crackles at the right base
steps.x: Chest signs point to a lung source.
A: Chest X-ray. Septic screen: CXR, urine and sputum culture, further imaging.

questions.stem: An 81 year old woman with sepsis from pneumonia has received a fluid bolus. The nurses are unsure how much urine she is passing because she is incontinent. Her BP is 96/58 mmHg and creatinine is rising.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate next step to assess her response to treatment?
questions.e: A urinary catheter allows accurate hourly input-output measurement, part of monitoring urine output in the Sepsis Six.

steps.x: Output cannot be measured accurately.

elim: Excludes obstruction, does not monitor output.

steps.x: B: Insert a urinary catheter. Catheter for accurate input-output in sepsis.

questions.stem: A 44 year old woman phones the GP surgery with fever and feeling very unwell after a dental abscess. The GP visits her at home. Before any tests are available, the GP needs to decide whether she has sepsis.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate initial assessment?
questions.e: Sepsis is first identified by immediate assessment of vital signs and clinical examination, then risk stratification (NICE NG51).

steps.x: No tests available yet.

elim: Not available at home and not the first step.

steps.x: E: Vital signs and clinical examination. Vital signs and examination come first.

questions.stem: A 69 year old man is diagnosed with sepsis from a urinary source in the emergency department. His BP is 92/56 mmHg and lactate 3.2 mmol/L. The nurse asks within what time frame the Sepsis Six bundle should be completed.
questions.q: Within which time should the Sepsis Six be completed?
questions.e: The Sepsis Six is completed within 1 hour; antibiotics are the single most important intervention.

steps.x: The question names the Sepsis Six.

elim: Too long; mortality rises with each hour of delay.

steps.x: A: 1 hour. Sepsis Six within 1 hour.

questions.stem: A 52 year old man has sepsis from community-acquired pneumonia. He has received oxygen. Blood cultures have been taken. His temperature is 39.1°C, pulse rate 118 bpm, BP 98/58 mmHg and respiratory rate 26 breaths per minute.
questions.q: Which is the single most important treatment?
questions.e: Antibiotics are the single most important treatment in sepsis, given within 1 hour.

steps.x: Cultures done; the cause must be treated.

elim: Not needed; he is not in fluid-refractory shock.

steps.x: A: IV antibiotics. Antibiotics are the most important sepsis treatment.

questions.stem: A 66 year old woman has sepsis from pneumonia. She is breathless. Her pulse rate is 118 bpm, BP 94/60 mmHg, respiratory rate 30 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 86% breathing air. She has no history of lung disease.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate initial management of her oxygenation?
questions.e: In the Sepsis Six give oxygen, 15 L/min via non-rebreathe mask if hypoxic.

steps.x: Hypoxic with no CO2 retention risk.

elim: For CO2 retainers, which she is not.

steps.x: A: 15 L/min oxygen via non-rebreathe mask. High-flow oxygen if hypoxic in sepsis.

questions.stem: A 75 year old man is drowsy with fever and a red, swollen arm around a cannula site. His airway is clear and breathing has been assessed. His temperature is 38.9°C, pulse rate 124 bpm, BP 86/50 mmHg and respiratory rate 24 breaths per minute. IV access has been obtained.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate fluid management?
questions.e: After airway and breathing, the ABCDE approach gives a 500 mL 0.9% saline bolus and reassesses.

clues: airway is clear and breathing has been assessed
steps.x: Hypotension after A and B are assessed.

elim: Glucose is not a resuscitation fluid.

steps.x: C: 500 mL 0.9% sodium chloride IV bolus. 500 mL 0.9% saline bolus, then reassess.

questions.stem: A 60 year old woman has sepsis from a perforated diverticulum with peritonitis. Blood cultures have been taken. She has no drug allergies. Her BP is 94/60 mmHg and lactate 3.8 mmol/L.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate empirical antibiotic regimen?
questions.e: Broad-spectrum IV cover of Gram-positive, Gram-negative and anaerobic organisms, e.g. piperacillin-tazobactam with metronidazole.

steps.x: A bowel source needs broad cover including anaerobes.

elim: Oral and does not cover anaerobes.
Only for lower urinary tract infection.

steps.x: A: IV piperacillin-tazobactam and metronidazole. Broad-spectrum IV antibiotics covering anaerobes.

questions.stem: A 58 year old man treated for sepsis with IV piperacillin-tazobactam is improving. On day 3 his blood cultures grow Escherichia coli sensitive to ceftriaxone and co-amoxiclav. His temperature is 37.4°C, pulse rate 88 bpm and BP 124/76 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the next most appropriate step in management?
o: Change to an antibiotic guided by sensitivities
questions.e: Empirical broad-spectrum antibiotics are adjusted once culture results are available.

clues: grow Escherichia coli sensitive to ceftriaxone and co-amoxiclav
steps.x: Sensitivities are now known.

elim: Too early; treatment must be completed.

steps.x: B: Change to an antibiotic guided by sensitivities. Narrow antibiotics to culture results.

questions.stem: A 70 year old woman with sepsis from pyelonephritis has had IV antibiotics and 2 L of 0.9% saline. Her BP remains 76/42 mmHg and lactate 5.0 mmol/L. Her chest has bibasal crackles.
questions.q: Which is the next most appropriate step in management?
o: Contact ICU to start a noradrenaline infusion
questions.e: Persistent hypotension unresponsive to fluids is septic shock and needs vasopressors such as noradrenaline in ICU.

steps.x: Fluid-refractory hypotension.

elim: Fluids have failed and crackles suggest overload.

steps.x: A: Contact ICU to start a noradrenaline infusion. Fluid-refractory hypotension: ICU for noradrenaline.

questions.stem: A 49 year old woman has sepsis from a 6 cm liver abscess seen on ultrasound. She has received 48 hours of IV antibiotics and fluids but remains febrile at 38.9°C with a pulse rate of 112 bpm and BP 104/64 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the next most appropriate step in management?
questions.e: Source control, draining abscesses and removing infected devices, is essential when antibiotics alone fail.

steps.x: A collection that antibiotics cannot sterilise.
D: Percutaneous drainage of the abscess. Source control: drain abscesses, remove infected lines.

questions.stem: A 67 year old man with sepsis from pneumonia has warm peripheries, a bounding pulse and BP 84/40 mmHg. His legs have become oedematous over 24 hours. A student asks what causes these features.
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism?
questions.e: A dysregulated immune response releases TNF-alpha and IL-6, causing widespread vasodilation, capillary leak and microvascular dysfunction.

steps.x: Vasodilation and leak together.

elim: Does not explain warm peripheries and leak.
Does not cause warm vasodilated shock.

steps.x: B: Cytokine-mediated vasodilation and capillary leak. Cytokines cause vasodilation and capillary leak.

questions.stem: A 56 year old woman with sepsis from cellulitis has a lactate of 4.4 mmol/L. After fluids it falls to 1.8 mmol/L. A student asks why the lactate rose.

visual.title: Serum lactate
visual.label: On arrival 4.4
visual.caption: Lactate above 4 mmol/L signals severe hypoperfusion.

questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism?
o: Reduced tissue oxygen delivery driving anaerobic metabolism
questions.e: Vasodilation and capillary leak cause relative hypovolaemia and poor oxygen delivery, driving anaerobic metabolism and lactate; its fall shows response to resuscitation.

steps.x: Fluids improved oxygen delivery and lactate fell.

elim: Lactate is mainly cleared by the liver.

steps.x: D: Reduced tissue oxygen delivery driving anaerobic metabolism. Lactate rises with anaerobic metabolism from hypoperfusion.

questions.stem: A 63 year old man with sepsis has serum albumin 22 g/L (35–50) and CRP 280 mg/L. He has no liver or kidney disease and no proteinuria.
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of his low albumin?
o: Hepatic synthesis diverted to acute-phase proteins
questions.e: The acute-phase response diverts liver protein synthesis to CRP at the expense of albumin.

steps.x: Normal liver and no losses, but very high CRP.
B: Hepatic synthesis diverted to acute-phase proteins. Acute-phase response lowers albumin.

questions.stem: A 71 year old woman with septic shock from peritonitis is on noradrenaline. An echocardiogram shows a reduced ejection fraction which recovers after a week. She had a normal echocardiogram last year.
questions.q: Which best explains why fluids alone could not maintain her BP?
questions.e: Vasodilation and myocardial depression from the inflammatory response overwhelm the circulation's capacity despite fluids.

clues: reduced ejection fraction which recovers after a week
steps.x: A transient fall in cardiac function during sepsis.

elim: Does not recover in a week.
Not the cause of shock here.

steps.x: E: Vasodilation with sepsis-induced myocardial depression. Septic shock = vasodilation plus myocardial depression.

questions.stem: A 59 year old man with septic shock has a mean arterial pressure of 55 mmHg after 3 L of IV fluid. A noradrenaline infusion is started and his MAP rises to 70 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of the improvement?
o: Alpha-1 mediated vasoconstriction restoring vascular tone
questions.e: Noradrenaline acts mainly on alpha-1 receptors to vasoconstrict and restore vascular tone lost in sepsis.

steps.x: BP rose only with the vasopressor.
A: Alpha-1 mediated vasoconstriction restoring vascular tone. Vasopressors restore vascular tone.
